title: Stress–strain and force–extension behaviour; Charge and current
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MT02-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MT02-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL01-1#N.3, EL01-1#N.6a, EL01-1#N.11, EL01-1#N.12.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Current
items.clue: Rate of flow of charge through a cross-section.

items.label: Coulomb
items.clue: Unit: the amount passing a place in a wire when 1 A flows for 1 s.

items.label: Elastic limit
items.clue: Largest force after which a wire still returns to its original length.

items.label: Hooke's law
items.clue: Statement that extension is directly proportional to the force applied.

questions.stem: In an electron beam in a vacuum tube, 1.5 × 10¹⁵ electrons pass through a cross-section of the beam in 8.0 s at a steady rate. What is the magnitude of the current in the beam? Use e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Predict first. A copper wire forms part of a circuit carrying a steady direct current. Which statement about the charge carriers in the wire is correct?

options.text: Free electrons drift slowly towards the positive terminal of the cell.
Electrons travel at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights at the instant the switch closes.
Protons move along the wire, from the positive terminal towards the negative one.
Electrons leave the cell and some are used up in the lamp, so fewer return to the cell.

questions.explanation: In a metal the charge carriers are free electrons. Being negative, they are attracted towards the positive terminal, and on average they drift only slowly (typically well under 1 mm s⁻¹).

questions.stem: Several wires meet at a junction in a circuit with steady currents. A student measures a current of 1.20 A in one wire leading into the junction, and currents of 0.70 A and 0.40 A in two wires leading out of it. The ammeters are ideal and read correctly. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The other wires at the junction carry a net current of 0.10 A away from it.
0.10 A of the current was used up as charge passed through the junction.
Charge is building up at the junction at a rate of 0.10 C each second.
An unmeasured wire must carry 2.30 A, the sum of the three measured currents.

questions.stem: A copper wire has a thick section X joined to a thin section Y, and there is a steady current in the wire. How do the currents I_X and I_Y in the two sections compare?

options.text: They are equal: the same charge passes each cross-section per second.
I_Y is greater, since the charges move faster through the narrow section Y.
I_X is greater, since the thick section X holds more of the charge carriers.
It depends on the direction of the current, as current decreases along a wire.
